title: Do You Need a Visa for Korea? K-ETA, Visa-Free Entry, and the New e-Arrival Card Explained (2026)
html:
Before you book a flight to Korea, there's some paperwork to think about — and it's easy to get confused, because the rules changed in 2026. Some travelers don't need a visa at all. Some don't even need K-ETA (a Korean online travel permit) right now. But almost everyone now needs a new online step called the e-Arrival Card. Here's what actually applies to you.

Do I need a visa to visit Korea?

Korea has visa-free agreements with more than 100 countries and regions. If your passport is on that list, you can visit for tourism without applying for a visa in advance — usually for stays of 30 to 90 days, depending on your nationality.

If your country isn't on the visa-free list, you'll need to apply for an actual Korean visa at a Korean embassy or consulate before you travel. There's no way to get one at the airport, so this has to be sorted out ahead of time. Since the exact list of countries and stay lengths is long and changes from time to time, the safest move is to check your own nationality on the Korean embassy or consulate website for the country you live in before you book anything.


Incheon Airport's Terminal 1 arrival hall — this is what greets you after immigration. Photo: Arne Müseler, CC BY-SA 3.0 DE, via Wikimedia Commons.

K-ETA: the online travel permit most visa-free visitors need

K-ETA (Korea Electronic Travel Authorization) is a short online form you fill out before you fly, similar to the US ESTA or Canada's eTA. Korea uses it to screen visa-free travelers before they board their flight, not after they land.

Here's the part that trips people up: citizens of 22 countries and regions are currently exempt from K-ETA, and this exemption runs through December 31, 2026. Those countries and regions are: Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Hong Kong, Italy, Japan, Macao, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Poland, Singapore, Spain, Sweden, Taiwan, the UK, and the US. If you hold one of these passports, you can currently skip K-ETA for a tourist visit (though you can still apply voluntarily if you prefer).

If your country is visa-free but isn't on that list (roughly 90 more countries fall into this group), you do need K-ETA. Apply only at the official site, k-eta.go.kr — some third-party sites charge extra fees to fill out the same free-to-file form for you. A few key details:

  • Cost: 10,000 KRW (roughly $7–8 USD), and it's non-refundable even if your application is denied
  • When to apply: at least 72 hours before departure — earlier is safer, in case there's a delay in processing
  • Validity: up to 3 years, or until your passport expires, whichever comes first, so you usually only need to do this once for several trips

One more thing worth remembering: this exemption is temporary. From January 1, 2027, K-ETA is currently set to become mandatory again for everyone, including travelers from those 22 exempt countries and regions.


Incheon Airport's Terminal 1 departure hall — K-ETA and the e-Arrival Card both need to be sorted out before you ever get here. Photo: Arne Müseler, CC BY-SA 3.0 DE, via Wikimedia Commons.

New in 2026: the mandatory e-Arrival Card

This is the part that even K-ETA-exempt travelers can miss. Since January 1, 2026, Korea requires every foreign visitor — tourists, business travelers, everyone, regardless of K-ETA or visa status — to submit an e-Arrival Card before entry. The paper arrival cards that used to be handed out on the plane are gone; this new online form replaces them completely.

The e-Arrival Card is a short form (your flight details, where you're staying in Korea, contact info) that you submit at the official site, e-arrivalcard.go.kr, within 72 hours before your flight. It's free. Once you submit it, you get a QR code — keep it saved and easy to find on your phone, because immigration staff check it when you land.

In short: even if your passport is one of the 22 that can currently skip K-ETA, you still can't skip the e-Arrival Card. Think of it as a completely separate, required step.


Entry and exit stamps from a trip to Korea. Photo: Sgroey, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Quick reference: what applies to you

Your situation Visa needed? K-ETA needed? e-Arrival Card needed?
Passport from one of the 22 K-ETA-exempt countries/regions (through Dec 31, 2026) No No (optional) Yes
Passport from another visa-free country (~90 more countries) No Yes Yes
Passport not on Korea's visa-free list Yes — apply at a Korean embassy/consulate ahead of time Not applicable (your visa covers entry) Yes

💬 Not sure which row applies to your passport? Tell me your nationality in the comments and I'll help you figure out exactly what you need!
meta_description: A beginner's guide to Korea's 2026 entry rules: who needs a visa, which 22 countries skip K-ETA through 2026, and why every visitor now needs an e-Arrival Card.
